title: The Last Errand Before the War
tease: He goes to ask for five villages instead of a kingdom, and everyone in the room has already told him what the answer will be.

audience.careNote: Nobody is hurt in this story — it stops before the war starts. But Draupadī asks him to remember her hair and the hands that seized it, and a child who asks what that means is asking about the dicing hall. Sātyaki says plainly that he wants the war. The weight of it is that the last attempt to stop it failed.

values: trying anyway when you have been told

blocks.text: Everybody in that room wanted something different, and only one of them was going to have to get into a chariot and go and say it out loud.
The brothers had come out of thirteen years away and asked for their kingdom. Then they had come down, and down, to five villages — four of them named and one left for the other side to choose.
The answer had already come back, before anybody set out, and it was about a needle.
«Kṛṣṇa» said he would go and put it to them in person.

In the city «Duryodhana» invited him to dinner, and he would not eat it. A messenger eats at your table after his errand has worked, he said, and not before. He went and ate at «Vidura»'s table instead.
It is a small thing and it tells you the whole of him. He had not come there to be anybody's guest.
«Vidura», who was on his side and loved him, said it plainly: do not go into that hall. They will not listen. You will be wasting your breath.
And this is the answer the story is kept for. If a man does everything he can to bring about a good thing, «Kṛṣṇa» said, and it fails — the good of having tried is still his.
So he went in, and asked, and every old man in the room asked with him. «Bhīṣma». «Droṇa». «Vidura». The blind king.
And when «Duryodhana» had stormed out of the court, his own mother was sent for, and he was fetched back in to hear her say it too.
He refused them all, twice, and the second time he said it to «Kṛṣṇa»'s face.
There was nothing left to do after that but go home and report it — which he did, word for word, so that it would be on the record for ever that somebody had asked.
Thirteen years were up. Twelve of them in the forest and the thirteenth spent in hiding, and the five brothers came back and asked for what was theirs.

They had already asked once. «Sañjaya» had come from the old king, and «Yudhiṣṭhira» sent his answer back with him. Not a kingdom. Five villages. Four of them named, and the fifth — pick any you like.
Give us five villages, he said, because we do not want this family destroyed.
And «Duryodhana» had answered it before anybody came, to his own father: he would not give up as much land as the sharp point of a needle could cover.
«Kṛṣṇa» said he would go himself, for the sake of both sides. Then the room argued.

«Bhīma», of all people, spoke for peace. He asked «Kṛṣṇa» to speak gently — not out of fear, he said, but to keep the family from being wiped out — and it startled everyone, as though the hills had lost their weight.

«Arjuna» said peace was worth proposing, then said what he thought: advice given to that man is seed sown where nothing grows. «Sātyaki» wanted the war, and the soldiers round him roared when he said so.
And «Draupadī» said: thirteen years I have kept this in my chest, like a fire that will not go out. Whatever else you do over there — remember my hair, and the hands that took hold of it.
He went. One night on the road, then «Hastināpura».
He greeted the blind old king and «Bhīṣma» first and the rest by age, then spent the afternoon with his aunt «Kuntī», who cried and told him what had been done to her sons.

«Duryodhana» invited him to dinner and he said no. A messenger eats at your table when his errand has worked, he said, not before; and a man does not eat the food of people who hate his friends. _Not from anger_, he said. _Not from spite._
He ate at «Vidura»'s house instead.
And it was «Vidura» — who was on his side, who loved him — who told him not to go into the hall. They will not listen. Whatever you say in there is wasted.
And «Kṛṣṇa» answered him. If a man does everything in his power to bring about a good thing and it comes to nothing, the good of the trying is still his.
And then, plainly, he added: having tried for peace, no king anywhere can blame me afterwards.

The text never says he knew it would fail — that is a later habit of retelling, and it makes the errand pointless. What it gives him is better: he was told it would fail, by someone who loved him, and he went and did it properly anyway.
So he went in, «Vidura» on one side and «Sātyaki» on the other. Hold your own sons, he said, and I will hold the five. There can be peace, and nobody need be killed for it.
«Bhīṣma» begged. «Droṇa» begged. «Vidura» begged. The father begged his son in front of the whole court.
And «Duryodhana» said it to «Kṛṣṇa»'s face, in front of all of them. Not as much land as the point of a sharp needle could cover. Then he walked out of the court.
«Gāndhārī», his own mother, was sent for, and he was fetched back in to hear her. He said the same thing again.
There was a plan to seize him and tie him up before he left. «Sātyaki» found out. «Kṛṣṇa» said he would do nothing blameable in return.

«Brahmā» at his forehead and «Rudra» at his chest. The guardians of the world along his arms, and fire and the gods out of his mouth. And round him — in a hall they were nowhere near — «Arjuna», «Bhīma», «Yudhiṣṭhira» and the twins.
The frightened kings shut their eyes. «Bhīṣma», «Droṇa», «Vidura», «Sañjaya» and the sages were given eyes to see it.
Then he walked out through the middle of them.

He came home and told them what he had said: that it was true, and reasonable, and good for the man he said it to, and that it had not been accepted. He had been told beforehand that it would not be. He said it anyway, so nobody could ever say it had not been asked.

close.question: Everybody told him it would not work before he went. Is there something you would still say?
close.seed: Some things are said so that nobody can ever claim afterwards that they were not asked.

ifTheyAsk.q: Did he know it would fail?
ifTheyAsk.a: The book does not say he knew. It says three things that sit next to knowing. Vidura told him his words would certainly be wasted. He himself told Arjuna that Duryodhana would not part with the smallest piece of the kingdom. And when Vidura pressed him, he did not argue that it might work — he argued that the attempt is worth making even when it does not. That is a different and a harder position than knowing the future, and it is the one the text actually gives him.

Ganguli's translation names four of them and leaves the fifth open — take any other you like. The four are Avishthala, Vrikasthala, Makandi and Varanavata in one passage, and the first of them appears as Kusasthala in another, so even the text is not perfectly steady about it. The tidy list of five you may find online, all ending in -prastha, is not the list the text gives, and we could find no early source for it — though Indraprastha, the first name on that list, is very much in the Mahābhārata as the brothers' own capital.

ifTheyAsk.q: Is this the same as the great form in the Bhagavad Gītā?
ifTheyAsk.a: No, though they are easy to confuse. The Gītā's comes later, on the battlefield, and is shown to Arjuna alone, who has to be given new eyes to bear it. This one is in a crowded hall, shown to a court in which four men had just agreed to tie him up, and the Pāṇḍavas appear inside it although they are not in that city at all. Two different moments, in two different books of the same epic.
